utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, I did understand that you would like to raise an issue in private session. May I take it that it's related to what we discussed yesterday at the very end of our session, where we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. Mr. Tieger and I both thought it would be better to briefly mention it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it also gives me an opportunity to state in public that we went into private session yesterday in relation with protective measures and that for that same reason we'll now turn into private session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, to add to the confusion, at line 9 the name there but so-and-so has written a book. It's the wrong name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I knew that, Your Honour, but my pronunciation of Serbian doesn't distinguish very well between the letters anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just -- good morning, Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, but before I give an opportunity for Mr. Stewart to continue his examination-in-chief, just for the parties, day 207 in my not-number-through transcript on page 89, second line, the book I just mentioned appears with an unclear name with it, but just for your information about sources. Perhaps I could -- perhaps I could ask the witness right away about it. Mr. Kecmanovic, did you write a book in which any -- in which the meeting of Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Izetbegovic are described? Or at least reference made to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. Not a book, certainly not. Maybe an article. You know, I have written a lot about those events. That is one of my permanent occupations, and I have published a number of articles on that. I'm not sure about the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we heard evidence that in one of your publications, let's say so, that meeting was situated in time on the 12th of April. We have not verified that, but -- on the basis of your publication, but that's at least what we received as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that I have mentioned the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, when you became a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, how frequently over -- it was a period of about five weeks that you were a member, how frequently did the Presidency meet?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency was in a state of permanent session, so to speak. We would meet in the morning hours and worked until lunchtime. Then we had a lunch break, and after that we would continue in the afternoon. We were sitting for several hours in the morning and again several hours in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you receive information during those meetings about military activities and operations in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not receive any specific conversation on war operations. I believe that the only person who received that information was Izetbegovic, but not the Presidency as a whole. The Chief of General Staff Halilovic would occasionally provide us with some general information, but that information was, in general terms, on the successes of the BiH army and the Muslim casualties at the hands of the Serb forces. That was general information which sounded non-authentically, and at one point Izetbegovic replied to the general: General, you keep on talking about your successes and all the while we're losing territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there any report or discussion at Presidency meetings about crimes committed by Serbs against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information was not precise. It was more of a general nature. And as a result of that permanent session, the work of the Presidency was very extensive. We talked about cooperation with UNPROFOR, our international position, support coming from abroad, the successes of certain units of BiH army, the situation in town. As a matter of fact, the Presidency had very little information as to what was going on outside of Sarajevo. The entire activity and all of the topics were more or less related to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any report or discussion about any prison or detention facilities of any sort within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pejanovic and myself informed the Presidency about that based on information that we received from the citizens who spoke to us on a daily basis. Other members of the Presidency never spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what -- what information did you convey to the Presidency on that topic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the time -- or rather, all the time outside the sessions the two of us would receive citizens and it would be mostly the Serb citizens who approached us, complaining of all sorts of ill treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Presidency receive any report or was there any discussion about activities of the JNA outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not about that. The general term used was "the aggressor," and then members of the Presidency of Muslim and Serb ethnicities understood that as the JNA, the Army of Republika Srpska, and all the other formations that were not under the command of the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some discrepancies there when it came to HVO units, which on the one hand acted independently and on the other hand in alliance with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any discussion or report at Presidency meetings about detention camps, prisons, any type of detention facilities away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It is possible. Pejanovic and I mostly focussed on private and official prisons in Sarajevo because Serb citizens complained that their closest relatives had been taken away and detained, that they did not have any information, that they had experienced their apartments being broken into, losing their jobs, ill treatment, beatings, and so on and so forth. In a way, we acted as protectors of the Serbian population that remained in the town, and in that sense we asked from the Presidency to take adequate measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did you finally leave Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened at the beginning of July 1992. To be more precise, I believe that this was on the 5th or the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I think it was on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the consent of President Izetbegovic and having informed Fikret Abdic of that, I went to this meeting in Lukavica with the representatives of the Serb side. I didn't know who exactly would be there. It was the late Professor Koljevic who met me in Lukavica. According to the previously agreed procedure, the UNPROFOR vehicle came to the Presidency and Izetbegovic's daughter informed me that they were waiting for me. I left the session, and in the UNPROFOR vehicle I went to the central base of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo. And from there Mr. McKenzie escorted me to Lukavica where I was met by Mr. Koljevic. That same evening I went to Pale, also escorted by --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I just wanted to get one thing clear to avoid any possible confusion. When you referred to this meeting in Lukavica, this is an entirely separate from the meeting you've described earlier in your evidence in Lukavica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- you met -- you said then at this later meeting you've been talking about you met Professor Koljevic. Were any other representatives of the Bosnian Serb leadership present?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was just Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- did you engage in a discussion with Mr. Koljevic there in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say what was the topic and content of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that it was always one and the same topic. It was always the same topic: How to stop the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were any specific proposals or possible solutions discussed?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long was the discussion between you and Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between half an hour and an hour. Now, in order to make it clear for you as to how it was possible for us to talk so long without any specific results of the talk, I must say that every conversation involved some private topics, because those people I had known before, some of them were my university colleagues, and I know that one of the topics that we discussed was the situation of the Serbian population in Sarajevo. In more specific terms, the brother of the late Professor Koljevic remained in town together with some members of his family, and he asked me if I knew anything about -- about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what was the point of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a Presidency session which had taken place before, I pointed to a stupid situation that the Presidency and the way it was functioning was in. I said that this was all very empty, without any purpose, because the Presidency was in some sort of isolation. Communication with other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina for all members of the Presidency save for Izetbegovic had been cut off. And at one point I said that we reminded of a ship of fools and that we should do something, that we should take a step towards communication with our surroundings. And in more precise terms, I said that this communication should be with the Serb side and the Croatian side, but not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also broader, and that it would be good if one of the Croatian members of the Presidency should go to Western Herzegovina and Zagreb, that one of the Serb representatives should go to Pale and Belgrade, and that we should be informed as to how things were outside of Sarajevo and what the political positions were on both sides. A special initiative for that were political changes that were taking place in Belgrade where Dobrica Cosic became president and Milan Panic became Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, after that meeting with Mr. Koljevic, did you report back to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to report to him, because after my meeting in Lukavica I went to Pale with Koljevic, and two days later I went to Belgrade. And I stayed in Belgrade after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you go to Pale on your own initiative or at anybody else's request or suggestion?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, my initiative was more in general terms, but the positions in the Presidency were different. Izetbegovic supported my initiative, and as far as I can remember, the Croatian representatives showed some reservations to any attempt at establishing connections between the Muslim and the Serb sides. However, after that meeting I spoke to Fikret Abdic, with whom I had rather good relations, and our offices were adjacent to each other, and I told him that I did not need the consent of the Presidency for such an activity because the Presidency was a collective body and I was equal amongst the many. And that the positions of the Croat representatives were not binding upon. In that sense, we spoke to Izetbegovic, who supported my initiative. And as a result of that, the communication with UNPROFOR and the organisation of my departure was in -- carried out by Mr. Izetbegovic's office. In addition to my contacts in Lukavica and Pale, I also had contacts in Belgrade along the same line --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's come to Belgrade in chronological sequence. So your trip to Pale was with some support or approval or encouragement from Mr. Abdic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Abdic and Izetbegovic, which is even more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how long did you spend in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in Pale for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the entire top leadership of Republika Srpska; namely, Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic, and Mr. Krajisnik. The Prime Minister wasn't there -- or maybe -- maybe yes. And also there were no military or police leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So did you -- those four people you've mentioned, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, did you talk to them together? Separately? Both together and separately?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, the situation in Pale was not regulated so as to provide for separate offices for those people, and there was no formal procedure in place. When I arrived, everybody was there. They were all gathered there in a small room where we had dinner together, and we held a conversation which was both formal and informal. And during the next couple of days, I had individual meetings with some of them. I spent most of the time in that room, and then somebody would come to that room, keep me company, leave; another person would come. It all depended on the work that was to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just for better understanding the testimony of the witness: You said you went to Lukavica, you went then to Pale, you went to Belgrade. Did you ever return to, well, let's say, Muslim-controlled Sarajevo in those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said something about the initiative. I did understand that you felt the need to communication with Pale/Belgrade, just as there was a need to communicate with the Croatian -- Zagreb. Now, to communicate doesn't mean that if you start talking with them, that you do not return. I -- I would have understood an initiative to communicate, that is, to speak with them, to talk with them, and then return back and see what to do with that. So therefore, the question put to you by

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- was it your own -- yes. He asked you: Did you go to Pale at your own initiative or at anybody else's request or suggestion? Then you answered very much in terms of what was needed as far as communication is concerned, but it doesn't answer the question as to who took the initiative not to return. I mean, going to Pale, going to Belgrade, and then not to return to Sarajevo. Could you tell us what made you decide - was it decided before you went or during the trip? - that you would stay in Serb-controlled area or in Serbia rather than to return to, well, your own Presidency in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left, as I said. I went in agreement with the leadership in Sarajevo, with Izetbegovic specifically. He was the person -- or rather, his office organised my departure from Sarajevo with UNPROFOR. Now, I decided to stay in Belgrade myself; I made that personal decision. And I informed -- I sent a fax to the Presidency or to Izetbegovic in person, actually, and I informed him of some of the elements of discussions I had had in Belgrade and the talks I -- well, I couldn't speak about the talks in Pale publicly. That would have been indiscreet. I also gave news agencies statements official statements from my talks with the president of Yugoslavia, who was Mr. Cosic, and Prime Minister Panic, and my meeting with the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church, Pavle. My decision to stay wasn't made straight away. I was rather hurt in Sarajevo -- or rather, I was injured in Sarajevo and went to Belgrade for treatment, and during that treatment I decided not to return anymore, and then I informed Sarajevo of that decision of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Mr. Stewart, please proceed. It was unclear to me when the witness decided not to return, whether it was in Lukavica or Pale or Belgrade, but it's clear to me now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, when you were in Pale, did you have any individual meetings, which I mean just the two of you, with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think that at a certain point Mr. Krajisnik did come in and we exchanged a few sentences but nothing specific. And Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic would come in in that same fashion. There certainly weren't any important exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say "come in," come in where or to whom?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would come into the room that I was in, the premises. To make things clearer, we conducted our talks that first evening when I arrived. However, since I asked to continue to Belgrade from Pale, I needed a certain amount of time to have my departure to Belgrade prepared. Quite obviously they weren't able to see to that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I was getting at, Mr. Kecmanovic, was when you said Mr. Krajisnik came in, or Mr. Koljevic came in, Mrs. Plavsic came in, do you mean come into a room where you were sitting, waiting, or come into a room where you were already there with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't sitting there, waiting. I wrote -- read all the newspapers that I didn't have an opportunity of doing in Sarajevo. I had taken some of my own papers and documents and notes, which I put into order. So it wasn't just waiting. I was able to move around, and I would leave the building from time to time, have a walk, got a bit of fresh air, had breakfast, and things like that. But that room, that premises -- those premises, the room I was in, where I was in most frequently was where they moved around. It's a relatively small area, small space. And as far as I was able to see, there wasn't any special room that was reserved for the president, the vice-president, the ministers, or anything like that. It was all very improvised, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have any proposals or positive suggestions that you were putting to the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale during that time you were there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, as opposed to my previous departures to the other side and the contacts, if I can put it that way, that I had and that I took part in, this time there was no specific agreement with the Presidency or the presiding person, who was Mr. Izetbegovic; it was more or less a mission not only to see the general mood and atmosphere on the other side. We wanted to find a way out of the situation, to see whether there were any political solutions, any ideas being put forward on those lines. So that on this occasion my aim, my reason for going, was not agreed upon by the members of the Presidency or Izetbegovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But that doesn't quite go to the point of my question, Mr. Kecmanovic. With all that, did you -- you, in fact, have any proposals or positive suggestions that you were putting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the -- told the Serbian leadership what the situation in Sarajevo was. I said that there was a very difficult humanitarian problem and that the Serb population was a group at risk in an otherwise very difficult situation and that it was the Serb population, the Serb inhabitants, that were hit hardest and that were under jeopardy most. And in order to ask them to do something for, of course, all the town's inhabitants but to make the situation easier particularly for the Serb population because I considered them to be additional -- I considered them to be the right people to see to problems of that kind since they had the legitimacy of the Serb people and the Serbian Democratic Party was a party that the Serbs voted for first and foremost. And for the party I represented, I assume there was a mixed voting from all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How much of the overall discussions that you had in Pale on that visit, as far as you can put some sort of percentage on it or give some guidance, how much of the discussion related to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of it. I would say 80 per cent of it. Or let me be more specific: I presented the difficulties, I explained the difficult situation in Sarajevo, and the other side gave me information about the very difficult situation around Sarajevo. And they warned and cautioned me that the artillery from Sarajevo was firing at Serb positions around town all the time, and I spoke about what I felt to be the situation in town, that the Serb artillery was targeting towards town. Then they warned me and said that the BH army -- or rather, the Muslim army artillery was within the city zones at the most sensitive points and that they were very often in a situation where they had to respond to the fire coming at them. Of course, the fire was concentrated in the locations from which the other side was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- was there any member of the Bosnian Serb leadership with whom you particularly discussed those matters that you've just mentioned; artillery placements in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody particular. As I said, there weren't [Realtime transcript read in error "were"] people there who dealt with military matters. Karadzic was there, who of course had the main say. He was the number one man of that leadership. Mrs. Plavsic would take part quite a bit as well, and Mr. Koljevic. Of course Mr. Krajisnik took part in the discussions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any discussion during that visit of yours to Pale about crimes committed in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific. It referred to the casualties, the victims, in a state of war, and that was a difficult situation generally. A component part were the casualties on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about detention facilities anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about private prisons in Sarajevo where Serbs were incarcerated and the opposite side did not tell me about the situation outside of Sarajevo. It all must sound a little restricted and -- but it must be borne in mind that I had those discussions some 10 or 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the point about the private prisons in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo a chaotic situation prevailed. The city was divided into zones controlled by some sort of paramilitary formations, and it was very difficult to determine their links to the powers that be, the authorities, and their relationship with the authorities. There were formations which were completely independent and which were in conflict with each other. Then there were other formations who had some formal ties with the authorities, but it wasn't quite clear how much they were under the authorities' control, whether they were or not. So these paramilitary formations, which sometimes behaved as military formations, sometimes as police formations and units, actually had power and authority in the various districts. They held power in their own hands, basically. They had their leader, or leaders. Those leaders were for the most part people whom I knew by sight. Some I knew from Sarajevo -- life in Sarajevo before the war, other people were along the fringes of society. They were bouncers in clubs, bars, people dealing in shady business, they were muscle men, things like that, and they were in power, they held power in their hands. They had their own units, armed formations, and among other things each of those districts and zones had their own prisons. The locations of those prisons were not officially recognised and officially known, but, quite simply, many people were taken to those places where they were abused, held for several days. Some people were never seen again; all traces of them was lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could I ask for a clarification of one of the previous answers of the witness. May I take you back to one of your previous answers. You were asked whether there were any members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. You particularly discussed those matters, and these were artillery fire, et cetera, with -- and then you said: "Nobody particular. As I said, there were people there who dealt with military matters. Karadzic was there." You mentioned Mrs. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter said not military matters, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I remember, Your Honour, I was going to comment. It was "not" as the introduction to that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear at this moment where this correction was made to line --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it was that -- it was part of that sentence. I understand the interpreter to be suggesting, Your Honour, that we're talking about the second sentence of that answer as it appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter who interpreted believes she said "not military matters," but she might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be in the line: "There were no people there who dealt not with military matters." Is that -- I'm looking at this moment at page 18, line 18 and 19. Is that what you're referring to at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I can say is that when I did the interpretation I seem to remember having said "not military matters," but whether I said "not," I can't be sure now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to that line --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My recollection is there were no people -- I certainly remember the negative sense of the sentence, Your Honour, because it would have struck me if it had not been that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So there was no one that dealt with military matters. Yes, that's my recollection as well. Then you mentioned Mr. Karadzic, whom you said he had a main say. You mentioned Mrs. Plavsic, who you said would take part quite a bit as well; and Mr. Koljevic. And then finally you said of course Mr. Krajisnik took part in the discussions as well. Would you mean that you would discuss with all of them in the absence of any, well, say specialists in military matters, that with the four persons mentioned you discussed these military matters? Is that how I should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite precise, what I said is this: I said there were not any military experts present, so we didn't speak about military matters specifically. But during the discussion there were those four people present, it was a conversation over dinner, and they took part in that conversation. Karadzic always had the main say as the most senior person by virtue of his position among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you say "the discussion," you're referring to the discussion about the Serb artillery and the Muslim artillery, which one had to respond or fired at, et cetera. That's that portion of the discussion you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you're nodding yes. For the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By the time you arrived in Pale on this occasion, had you heard news or suggestions that there was ill treatment of civilians in Bosnia and Herzegovina in any form of detention facility?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was mention of that in the reduced media and the war-oriented propaganda, and in the Presidency as well. But there was never any specific, precise information about it. There was general talk about that, that there was suffering, that many civilians had lost their lives because there was fighting going on on all sides, and that the Muslim people were suffering first and foremost, that their houses had been burnt, that many had been killed. But they were not detailed, precise pieces of information. It was talked about as if the whole of the surrounding parts of Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina was in the flames of war in which everything was ablaze, in which people were losing their lives, and things like that, but not any precise, specific information coming in to us in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you first arrived in Pale on that occasion in July, based on everything you'd heard and discussions in the Presidency, whatever news you'd received, did you believe yourself at that point that there was a problem about war crimes, ill treatment of civilians in any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: I had direct access just in Sarajevo, but everything else that I could have heard was second-hand information and prejudice, just as the information that I listened to from Radio Pale were biased. And I said in our talk yesterday that the perception by the population was such that one side accepted just one set of information, the other side accepted another set of information, and the two sides didn't believe in these various sets of information being put out. As far as I can see, I realised that the truth was not on any one side. It was war and there were casualties on all sides because that's a component part of war, suffering and destruction on all sides. And apart from that, it was a civil war; therefore, it could only have been worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was your personal belief that things were happening which were worse than inevitably to be expected in a civil war and things were happening that were war crimes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll take it in stages, Mr. Kecmanovic. What you said is correct, is it, you had a clear personal conception of what inevitably would happen in a civil war; that there would be terrible harm to people and property. That was clear, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kecmanovic, at that time you -- can we take it you also -- not necessarily with legal precision, but you also had yourself some clear concept of things which were not permissible in war, particularly in relation to treatment of civilians. You had a clear idea of that distinction, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time I didn't deal with the international legal aspects of war crimes, nor any laws on war. But what I can tell you is this, from my own experience in Sarajevo, which was my direct experience: You know, people who some -- who a month before or one or two weeks before behaved in the kind of way that I had been used to, they were my friends, my neighbours, my colleagues at work, we had normal relationships and more than that. Overnight, however, this mood changed, the general atmosphere changed, and you could see changes in the course of the day, as the days passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, until now it's not an answer to the question. The question was whether at the time you had yourself some clear concept of things that were permissible or not permissible. Then you said you did not deal with the international legal aspects of crime. I do understand that. But did you know what was forbidden even without studying the international law aspects? Some people, without ever having seen a law, know that it's not permitted to kill your neighbour, as where -- so even such a knowledge, such an awareness, may exist even without studying the law. Were you aware of that and specifically what was permissible to civilians and non-civilians? Did you have any awareness of that? I think that was the question, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can tell you is this: Practically everything that happened around me in Sarajevo came into the category of impermissible acts, fell into that category, impermissible things. However, before that I said that that was a completely deregulated state. I was a member of the state Presidency, for example; however, I was not able to be fully informed or certainly not to control or influence events in the district in which I lived, for instance. Starting from that, and then everything else was abnormal and could have been -- people were taken -- could have been considered reprehensible. People were taken away, they were incarcerated. All traces were lost of that. The divisions, ethnic decisions, were impermissible in a situation like that, but it was a chronic state in Sarajevo during that time. Of course, the fact hat it was chronic doesn't change anything in evaluating the situation and sizing it up. When I said I didn't deal with the legal aspects, I said that a little ironically, I was being ironic, but of course everything that happened was not actually permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You made a distinction before between I would say private gangs and what you saw to be impermissible. Was that exclusively behaviour of private gangs or did you also discern impermissible behaviour, from whatever side, not committed by private gangs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. In addition to those private gangs, there were those who had the insignia of the official army or police, the BH army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they too engaged in impermissible acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I said before from both sides. Did you observe any impermissible acts by the opposite armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that I did do was hear about this, and this referred to artillery fire that came into town from up on the hill. That was something that somebody living in town was present in a very direct manner; otherwise, I didn't have any other contacts with the other side. I didn't have any immediate experience as to what was happening outside town, but the situation in town is -- was as I have described it to you. There was artillery fire from the surrounding hills, which was held -- which were held by the Serbs. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what you saw, and I now refer to what Mr. Stewart earlier asked of you, from the level of awareness you had on what was permissible and not permissible in war, the effects of artillery from the hills, as you said, did that give you the impression that it was all permissible or did you also gain the impression that some of this fire was impermissible? Just to give you an example: If you see a -- let's just assume a tank being hit by a missile, my first impression would be that the missile attacked a clear military object, being a tank, whereas I can imagine other situations where the effects of the artillery fire would not be obviously permissible or perhaps give an impression of being impermissible. From what you observed in town, did you gain any such impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not difficult for me to answer that question of yours at all. I was down in the town myself, so I was a potential victim of that artillery fire. So that is also something that I experienced very directly, and I risked my life on a daily basis being there. But I wasn't able to assess, nor am I an expert in the field, of whether a projectile coming from the hill had missed a target, missed a military target, for instance, and then hit something else or not. All I can say and all I know is that that firing did exist, there was shooting, and there were people who fell victim to that shooting, and that I, myself, moving around town might have been hit by the same token. And most of the citizens stuck to their own homes or didn't leave town much. I moved around. So they were trying to protect themselves, but for my job I had to move around town all the time, leave my home. And all this was a risk. It was an adventure that you undertook that you could have paid for with your life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would one be safe if one would stay at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, because they were projectiles which were not -- didn't have the explosive force and power to destroy houses. So if you were indoors, in a house, especially if you were in a more secure part of the building -- you see, mostly - and I did this myself when I was at home, as did my family - we were in rooms that were facing the front -- or rather, we weren't in the rooms facing the front. We were in the back rooms that were not facing the outside world, if I can put it that way. And the best places for rallying were the landings between the apartments, between the flats. Everybody would congregate there on these landings and they became a sort of joint sitting room because that was considered to be the safest place, these landings between the flats. And some of the inhabitants in the buildings who were more afraid and who didn't have nerves that weren't that strong went to cellars and basements and took refuge there. I myself was not able to ensure that safety for myself because I just had to go to work every day and come back home from work. I had a job to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand you well to say that if you'd stay at home, that if you'd stayed at the side of your home that was not exposed to -- to fire, that then you would be relatively safe but you should take the precaution not to stay at the exposed side because you were not safe there. At least there was a risk not to be ignored of firing reaching the home or the apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that my apartment was specifically targeted, but you know that in artillery activity you can't -- when artillery fire was opened, we as civilians didn't know what their targets were. In addition to that, there were artillery batteries in defence of town that were deployed in different places, and there would often be return fire. But that fire was not very precise and there was no guarantee that a shrapnel wouldn't fall close or that a shell would miss and that it wouldn't fall close to where we were. It did happen. It was known to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, in the course of your visit to Pale, did you ever suggest to any of the Bosnian Serb leadership there that they or anybody under their control had crossed the line from between legitimate conduct of war and criminal conduct of war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Professor Kecmanovic, let's lay some groundwork then. We can agree -- let's say -- use His Honour's example that normally speaking if you see a tank taken out, there's a very strong presumption that that's a legitimate military activity; unfortunately, though, the entire circumstances of the situation are it's part of conduct of a war. We can understand that. Agreed? You have to say something into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can also agree, can't we, that take the most terrible things, if you send millions to extermination camps and kill them, that's plainly, utterly, illegal. Everybody knows that, don't they?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Somewhere between those extremes, there's a line, hard to define with precision, but you understand -- we understand the concept of there being a line, Mr. Kecmanovic. Correct? That's all I'm seeking your agreement --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in theory and in reality, in practice, Mr. Kecmanovic, there is such a line, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me. Ten or 15 years later, as I sit here in the courtroom, it is very different to discuss those things, especially your views are different. I remember the situation well, even after those 10 or 15 years. On both sides those were town neighbourhoods, and when there is artillery on both sides targeting town neighbourhoods, everything is so close to each other and it is very difficult to achieve such an ideal situation so as to hit your exact target. Even if the hits were precise, there was still collateral damage because those artillery nests were between the buildings. And as far as I know, this is not only on this side but on the other as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm not making myself clear here; that's plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I think we could cut matters short. Because lengthy discussion on whether lines are there in theory only and how it worked out, I think the core of your question was, and I'll put it to Mr. Kecmanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just comment this, Your Honour: I'm informed that the translation into B/C/S is not regarded as clear by the B/C/S speakers, which I think I include Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Sladojevic. I just raise that concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general or a specific point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I haven't discussed with him what the specific point is, but I can do, Your Honour. It clearly relates to this most recent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we do the following: I try again to put the question as I understand it to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and see what the relevance still is of any imprecision in earlier translation. Mr. Kecmanovic, I think Mr. Stewart wanted to know whether you ever said to your interlocutors in Pale: Be aware that what happens in the war is not only horrible but even goes beyond what would be permissible in a war? Did you ever say such a thing to your interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember having said that, but I thought that this was implied, that it goes without saying, that they were aware of that just as I was. We were in a territory that was not large. They were in one part of the town; I was in another part of the town. Sarajevo itself was divided into two parts; a smaller part of the new part of town with the Serb forces, and the other side where the Muslim forces were predominant. The distance was not that big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it goes without saying that they were aware of that, just as I was, were you referring to a way of conducting hostilities which was impermissible even in war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is absolutely inadmissible. There is no doubt about that. But those things happened in both parts of the town. Let me be more precise. There is a river flowing through town; its name is Miljacka, and in some parts of town only Miljacka separated the two sides and the artillery fire was opened on both sides and the consequences of that artillery fire was the same on both sides. Therefore, I could not tell them anything new. I could not inform them of anything they didn't know already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still not entirely clear, Mr. Stewart. At the same time, the witness said he never raised such an issue but he thought they would be aware, just as he was aware. And then we get a few lines which might not demonstrate precise and full awareness of where the lines should be drawn in a combat situation. Of course if you want to further explore the matter, fine, but it's certainly that the matter has not been raised by the witness, that seems to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm not going to carry the topic further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock and I'd like to -- ask Madam Usher, first of all, to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just for scheduling purposes, what could we expect in today, perhaps even tomorrow? You indicated that next witness would not -- you couldn't start the next witness until Thursday, but what is our perspective?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as this witness is concerned, when we -- when we leave Pale, which we should do quite soon, we go very briefly to Belgrade and then I'm going to tidy up as best I can, Your Honour, those issues relating to the meetings that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The itinerary would take you how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it's only those topics, Your Honour. Within half an hour, I would suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we know what to expect approximately. We will adjourn and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I've handed in to the Court through the Registry an extract from a book. Your Honours may be familiar with it. I have a copy of the book in court for reference. It's -- the author is Glenny --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who is, from what I remember, a British journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He is, Your Honour, correct. And it's called "The Fall of Yugoslavia." I have the third edition with a new epilogue, third edition, 1996. Your Honour, in accordance with the usual practice, I've put a couple of pages around it for context, but the whole book is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you want to exhibit this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour, and I'm going to -- of course it's in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar -- I take it just the pages you presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just the extract is all I'm proposing and the book is, of course, available.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one particular paragraph, it's about 15 lines, it's at page 202 and it begins with the words: "Nenad Kecmanovic." So that indicates why that paragraph is the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a good start for the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's certainly a good start for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, forgive me if I don't hand it to you because it's simply going to be translated for you from the English into your own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for that to be done. It is only about 15 lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to ask for a short intervention, as I believe that before the break I was not clear in what I said. May I please have the floor to say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When I mentioned that the Serbian leadership was in a position to know what the situation was and that I didn't think it necessary for me to ask them or to tell them anything. I gave you the example of the Miljacka river as a small stream and I said hat it was a separation of the two parts of the city of Sarajevo. Those two parts of Sarajevo are very close to each other. They're only separated by bridges. On the one side there was the Serbian population, and on the other side there was the Muslim population. The Muslim artillery opened fire on the Serbian part of town and vice versa. And the same sequelae that I felt in my part of town from the Serb artillery, the same sequelae must have been on the other side as a result of the Muslim artillery. In both cases the artillery fire was opened on densely populated areas. And this is what I meant when I said that they must have been aware of the consequences because they themselves suffered the same consequences at the hands of the other party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I should say, Mr. Kecmanovic, that the passage I'm inviting the interpreters to deal with, I am going to ask you whether you agree with it, whether there's anything in it that you disagree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether it would be helpful for Mr. Kecmanovic just to have a piece of paper and make any notes while he listens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought perhaps that might. That's completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're an author, you need a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think so. Do you -- thank you very much. Is Your Honour then ready for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm ready to. You'll read it yourself, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean somebody has to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Nenad Kecmanovic served for a short time after the war had erupted on the Bosnian Presidency. In August of 1992, he travelled to Belgrade with the approval of President Izetbegovic to hold talks with Slobodan Milosevic although he never returned to Bosnia. En route, he stopped off at the Serb headquarters in Pale when I spent a boozy evening with him and Nikola Koljevic, Karadzic's deputy."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just pause there. It says "August 1992," Mr. Kecmanovic, whereas you have told us early July 1992. Does the date August in the book there cause you to reconsider or do you wish to stick with what you had told the Trial Chamber about the date?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- actually, I'm sure that this information is wrong. I am not disputing what he says here, but Mr. Glenny, whom I met and whom I saw in Belgrade, never checked this with me. And it is also not true that I went to talk to Milosevic. I didn't meet with Milosevic at the time. I met with Cosic, Babic [as interpreted], and Patriarch Pavle. And a third thing, if that is at all important, I was not the one who drank, and maybe that is why I remember so well what happened. It is true that we dined together and that this dinner lasted for a while - all the evening, as a matter of fact - and that Professor Koljevic was with the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where would -- can you say how Mr. Glenny, the author, might have got the idea that Koljevic was Mr. Karadzic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember how it looked in particular stages, but I know that at a certain stage there was the Presidency of Republika Srpska. Karadzic was the president of that Presidency, and the others were members of the Presidency. And then in the second stage he was president and they were vice-presidents. And by being a vice-president, together with Mrs. Koljevic [as interpreted], actually he was number two. He actually shared place number two with Mrs. Plavsic, and I believe that in that sense this was true, or was said like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 36, line 9, the second name there, Babic, Your Honour, the witness said Panic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's now corrected for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then continuing the text here. "Kecmanovic was in a state of depression and anger as the Bosnian Serb news agency, SRNA, had blown his cover and reported erroneously that he had fled Sarajevo for his safety, having arrived in Pale 'in a very poor physical condition' (which implied that he had been beaten up by Muslims)." Do you agree with or otherwise comment on that passage?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What specifically don't you agree with?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with two of the three things. I don't agree with the statement that I fled Sarajevo; to the contrary, I went very officially, very openly. I also don't agree that I had been beaten up in Sarajevo; that is absolutely not correct. And I can only agree with the allegation that I was depressive, but this feeling was common to all the citizens during the war and -- and political leaderships on the three sides were not immune to that. But what might have created an -- a stronger impression of that was the fact that I was not prepared to talk to the journalists who were up there, although I knew all of them from before the war. I simply believe that my stay there should have been as discreet as possible. I was angry that the information had leaked because that part of my journey should have become secret in agreement with Izetbegovic. The contacts between the two sides, as a rule, were secret because the grassroots did not look upon -- favourably upon such meetings when I arrived in Belgrade. In Belgrade, people had a different opinion about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, there may not be disagreement here, because you don't have advantage of the text, but in fairness to the author he is saying that it had been reported erroneously that you had fled Sarajevo and that you had arrived in a very poor physical condition. You appear to agree with the author that that report was wrong. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then it continues: "During the course of the evening --"

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I simply did not hear this no or negative sentence in the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it continues: "During the course of the evening, he --" and that's you, Mr. Kecmanovic -- "he cheered up a little and said to Koljevic: 'You know, you are all too personally involved with Sarajevo and I think that is why you spend so much time on it.' 'Yes,' Koljevic nodded his head sagely as is appropriate for the leading Serbo-Croat translator of Shakespeare. He then added absent-mindedly as an afterthought, 'Of course with everybody worrying about Sarajevo, it means that they don't pay much attention to what's going on elsewhere.'" That's a number of years ago, Mr. Kecmanovic, but does that ring true, did some such exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course when it comes to more subtle things, my memory doesn't serve me that well. It's easier for me to either confirm or refute some specific things. I don't think that this is very precisely put. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it your view that the -- all the people in Pale were too personally involved with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might say so, and I was no exception. I believe that I said it in the first person plural. Like on so many occasions during my testimony, you have often asked me about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and I have told you every time that I am familiar with the situation in Sarajevo. We were all focussed on Sarajevo because we resided there and Mr. Koljevic was not born in Sarajevo but in Bosnian Krajina in Banja Luka. But he spent most of his time in Sarajevo; that's why all of our conversations focussed on Sarajevo and things that were happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I finished with that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have nothing more on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, you then -- you then went straight from Pale to Belgrade by plane. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not by plane but by helicopter. There was one offer on the table -- actually, there was a discussion as to how we would go to Belgrade and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kecmanovic, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I believe it is important --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you said it's important. If it's important to explain how you got to Belgrade, please do.

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe not, but I'll be brief: There was a proposal for me to go with Mr. Karadzic by helicopter, which was supposed to leave immediately. But that was a helicopter carrying wounded, and since I was no longer popular amongst the Serbs because I was on the other side, I believed that this might have been rather awkward, so I opted for the second variant, which was for me to leave on the following day in a smaller helicopter with Mr. Koljevic. And this is what transpired, and that's why I stayed a day longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale regard you as being on the other side?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very complex question, and the answer is both yes and no. I can't answer otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... can you answer it, in the first place, in relatively simple terms, Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it will be more precise to try and describe the situation from my point of view and how I view the leadership in Pale. On the one hand this was the other side to the conflict, as I have already mentioned. I was in the town of Sarajevo and I was at a risk from the Serb artillery. However, at the same time those were my fellow nationals, people whom I knew well before the war. And as I told you yesterday very explicitly, I believed that the event in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina when the Serb side was over voted, which was a huge injustice, that that was an immediate political introduction to the war. And this had -- this had made my position very relative to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in -- in bare terms, were you regarded by Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders in Pale as being on the other side in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say that they considered me as a person who is on the other side but is not their enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In Belgrade you said whom you met. Did anything of practical usefulness emerge from the discussions you had in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to talk about any practical use. In any case, those talks had more content than the talks in Pale. In my conversation with Dobrica Cosic, Professor Koljevic attended one part of that conversation. Then Dobrica Cosic, with whom I found common grounds, unlike with Koljevic, then Cosic asked Koljevic to leave us alone. Cosic was very concerned and worried when I told him some things. He was very depressed. At some points I could even notice that he perceived the situation even worse than I who had been there. He showed more desire to help me. He noticed that I had pain in my back, and he made sure that I was given medical attention. My back pain was the result of the time spent in Sarajevo. I will go back to that if necessary. As for my meeting with Panic, the situation was absolutely different. Panic exuded optimism, great optimism. With regard to the situation, he thought things could be resolved quickly. And on the one hand he really changed me with his optimism, but on the other hand I realised that he did not understand the situation. I tried to make his optimism more realistic. He was talking about buying out weapons from all the three sides, approaching the matter in a very business-like manner. And I told him that people were buying more rather than selling weapons. I told him that I would like to join in his optimism if there was good reason for it. As for my conversation with Patriarch Pavle, we spoke in general terms. He is a very deeply religious person, and in our conversation he made a lot of reference to the Holy books. As for my concrete proposal that the episcopate of Bosnia who was in charge of the general area of Sarajevo to come to Sarajevo, the -- his predecessor had died and he was just appointed in Belgrade. I asked for this new episcopate to come to Sarajevo because that would mean a lot, not only for the Serbs and the followers of the Orthodox religion, but for all the citizens it would have been a symbolic sign that the situation was calming down. However, the patriarch told me that such a decision is beyond his power and that I should talk to the episcopate himself. And then he organised a meeting for -- between me and the episcopate in the church building. And in a nutshell, that would be the long and the short of all the three conversations that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said that you felt -- you realised that Mr. Panic did not understand the situation. That's page 41, lines 19 and 20. Apart from what you indicated about buying and selling of weapons, can you say what else you realised Mr. Panic did not understand about the situation?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the impression that he was looking at things in more simple terms and that he was simplifying them, although they were not simple at all. At one point he told me: The two of us, we'll go there together, and then we will resolve the situation very quickly. The war had already been under way, and in Sarajevo I had witnessed the growing hatred among the people, and I was absolutely clear that things would not be that simple to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you report back to anyone in Sarajevo the outcome of your discussions in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I knew that I would be hospitalised in the next few days, I sent faxes -- a fax to Izetbegovic, and then I gave the press my written statement very briefly, without any elaboration, and that statement went through Tanjug to other press agencies, as is customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you report the outcome of your discussions in Belgrade to anyone in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you involved in any further political activity in relation to conflict from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll allow me, I've just remembered that with Prime Minister Panic, who was a very pragmatic person, I agreed to open another blue way. In that time that meant communication on the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the delivery of humanitarian aid. And as to your question, I can say that after that until this very day I have withdrawn from any political activity. My hospital stay gave me ample time to ponder upon things, and it was then that I decided that I would no longer engage in politics, save for maybe only marginally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of circumstances in which Serbs left Sarajevo in any significant numbers?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was very specific when it came to the departure of Serbs from Sarajevo. There was a kind of permanent ethnic violence. I've already spoken about that. Serbs were not allowed to leave Sarajevo, although a majority of them wanted to do that. But there were ways if you had money, or if you ceded your apartment, to leave town with the help of paramilitary or police forces. And people paid a lot of money in foreign currency to save themselves and to leave town. Some tried to do that without such help and they lost their lives on the separation line, or when they tried to leave they were caught and punished because general mobilisation was in place, and any attempt to leave the city of Sarajevo was considered a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you at any time - and I mean at any time from 1992 onwards - hear anything about Mr. Krajisnik advising or encouraging Serbs to leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you hear such a thing at any time; during or after the war?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. During the war I believe that the Serb side, but not Mr. Krajisnik personally, launched an initiative to allow the citizens of Sarajevo of Serb ethnicity to leave town, not only Serbs but people of all origin. The advantage was to be given to the elderly, to the sick, women, and children. And it was said that they would guarantee safe passage through the territory under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I want to return to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one clarifying question. Your last answer says that you believed that the Serb side launched an initiative to allow the citizens of Sarajevo of Serb ethnicity to leave town. Was that to allow citizens to leave or had it anything to do with the Serbs having to allow Muslim citizens to leave Serb-controlled areas? Well, I mean, was this just one-sided or was it an exchange, something like an exchange, you are -- you heard about or what you said you believe? I don't know on what your belief is based.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This was information that arrived through the media. I've already said that in Sarajevo on the Muslim side we could follow the Serb media from the Serbian part of the town of Sarajevo. There was an urban area on the Serb side, and we could listen to the Serb radio. And through the media I believe that Karadzic himself, live on radio, invited the town of Sarajevo to allow the citizens of Sarajevo who wanted to leave town and that the Serb side would allow them safe passage through the territory controlled by them. This applied primarily to the elderly, to women with children. This was an invitation to all of those who wished to leave town. And let me add to that: This was not in terms of any exchange, although there -- there were such arrangements as well, but in this particular instance, that was not the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were -- this was a call upon the Sarajevo town authorities to let Serbs go who wanted to leave. Are you aware in any way of freedom of Muslims to leave --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And others, yes. Are you aware of the freedom of Muslims and others to leave the Serb-controlled area and to move to the city of Sarajevo or to move to any other Muslim-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember, and my knowledge on what you've just asked me is rich but not immediate and not from that period of time. I heard about that after the war when people told me about their experiences throughout the war, but what I can tell you as an eye-witness from the time when I was in town, that's in the early 1990s when the war had just started, I can only say that during the first few months of the war it was relatively easy for Muslims to cross from the Serb-controlled area to the Muslim-controlled area and vice versa. For example, Grbavica is one of the neighbourhoods in Sarajevo that was on the Serbian side, and I know some people who moved with their family members on the Muslim side. And I also know some Serbs who crossed over to the other side. But that was just during the first few months when it was possible or not that difficult. Later on it became more and more difficult to the point when it became absolutely impossible to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be more specific on that point in time when it became more difficult. When you left - you said that was early July - was it then still possible to move out freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could you please then tell us when approximately this became a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that already at the beginning of May it was almost impossible. But in April it was still doable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic, I want to return to the meetings that you described which involved Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Pejanovic, and in different combinations Dr. Karadzic. You described one meeting in Ilidza and then another meeting some weeks later, apparently, in Lukavica. Was there ever a meeting in 1992 involving you, Mr. Pejanovic, and either or both of Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic at the Hotel Serbia in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that you are relying on Pejanovic's book. He made a mistake. I don't think it was intentional. There is no reason for him to make an intentional mistake. As far as I can remember that book, he describes it as two meetings, one of which was at the Terme Hotel in Ilidza involving Karadzic and Krajisnik, and he combined that with a meeting in Lukavica with Mr. Krajisnik. He gave me that book of his, and I pointed the mistake to him. He wrote the book much later, and this was a genuine mistake on his part. There was no meeting at the Serbia Hotel, which is also in Ilidza. The meeting -- the only meeting was at the Terme Hotel, and that meeting involved Karadzic, Krajisnik, Pejanovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that a single meeting or was it a meeting that was split over more than one day?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a brief meeting. As I already said yesterday, it lasted less than an hour; half an hour, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And during the course of that meeting, did Mr. Krajisnik discuss the question of ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What would you -- from your being there in 1992, what would be your comment on any suggestion that Mr. Krajisnik had developed any sort of obsession about ethnic division in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see: One could say that the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina was -- well, I won't call it anybody's obsession, but it was -- that it was the prevailing topic in all political talks, that is a fact, and that was the concept of the European Union ultimately as well, which Cutileiro, as a representative of Europe, proposed. It was a topic I dealt with myself as one of the participants of one of the sessions which was chaired by Cutileiro in Sarajevo, and it was a topic that I dealt with in my party, as I mentioned yesterday, and I introduced elements of that into our party platform. And that was something that was just simply on the agenda, in the Assembly, in the government, in the media, in the political parties, and so forth. I don't mean that Mr. Krajisnik was somebody who especially dealt with the subject, but I remember during that period of time also, for instance, that wherever you would attend a meeting, the people there had before them the Swiss constitution, the Belgian political system. So a quest was underway for analogies and to apply parts of that in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there --

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in my party people who dealt with this specifically and served as some sort of expert -- experts to provide us with reliable data in the matter. Mr. Cutileiro, for instance, had an associate by the name of Mr. Darwin, who was with him all the time, and as far as I remember he was a specialist in cartography, for instance. And he was always in charge of explaining the separation lines, demarcation lines, and what it would look like on a geographic map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- and I don't need to distinguish between the two meetings that you've referred to, one in Ilidza, one in Lukavica, so we can -- this question can apply to either or both of those meetings. Was there a difference of view between you and Mr. Pejanovic on the one hand and Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic on the other hand on the question of whether the Bosnian situation could or should be resolved by force as opposed to by negotiations?

utterances.speaker: NENAD KECMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that respect, absolutely not. Everybody, of course, not only in declarative terms, but really did prefer favourised political negotiations.
